chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: 'The job is yours. We leave at 9': scrambling to join Jordan
summary: With his wife in hospital and two children at home, he gets Jordan's Monday call and has to arrange childcare and race across town.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: In the meantime, it was one of those kind of rough periods, and she had an operation, which cost about five hundred dollars -- and five hundred dollars at that particular time was a nice sum of money. And I was home with my two

kids. So on the weekend, I'm hoping that Louis Jordan is going to call sometime, so I can make arrangements, if I have to leave town, for my two kids to stay either with my mother-in-law or some aunts or something. So I waited over the weekend, and I didn't hear anything.

So that Monday morning, I was in bed, and at what must have been around o'clock I got a call. And it was Louis Jordan. Louis Jordan had a thing where he called everybody "Daddy." He said, "Hey, Daddy, the job's okay. The job is yours." I said, "Good, so what are we doing." He said "We're leaving at 9 o'clock for some town in North Carolina." "Gee," I said, "I've got to make arrangements to get a place for my kids to stay and to just clean up a few things around here" -- and I gave him the story of what was happening. It sounded like a rather cold statement, but what he said was, "Well, you got the job, Daddy. We're leaving at 9 o'clock. If you want it, be there." So I made a mad rush to pack clothes, get the kids somewhere, and telephone calls and whatever. The place they were leaving was Fifteenth and U Streets Northwest, and I lived on Fifty-Second Street Northeast, which meant that with a fast taxicab, you could make it in about 35 or 40 minutes.
